content: 1. Gnosis refers to the testing of infants to determine their HIV status. This is crucial because HIV can be transmitted in utero (during pregnancy), peripartum (during delivery), postpartum (through breastfeeding), or via parenteral exposure. 2. The eclipse period is the time between HIV infection and the detection of virological markers such as HIV RNA/DNA or the HIV p24 antigen. 3. Enhanced patient referral involves a trained provider using various tools to help HIV-positive clients disclose their status and offer HIV testing services (HTS) to their partners. These tools may include written information, leaflets, referral slips or cards, anonymous web-based messaging, or providing HIV self-testing kits for partners to test themselves. 4. External quality assessment is an inter-laboratory comparison to ensure that HIV testing services provide accurate test results and diagnoses. 5. False reactivity occurs when a specimen initially shows a reactive result but cannot be confirmed upon repeat testing with the same or a different assay. 6. A generalized epidemic is when HIV is firmly established in the general population. While high-risk subpopulations may disproportionately contribute to the spread, sexual networking within the general population is sufficient to sustain the epidemic. 7. A numerical proxy for a generalized epidemic is when HIV prevalence consistently exceeds 1% among pregnant women attending antenatal clinics. 8. Harm or social harm refers to any physical, economic, emotional, or psychosocial injury caused intentionally or unintentionally by one person to another, by a person to themselves, or by an institution to a person, occurring before, during, or after HIV testing. 9. HIV positivity is the percentage of people tested for HIV who are determined to be HIV-positive. A high positivity rate suggests that HTS is effectively targeted. 10. HIV self-testing is a process where an individual collects their own specimen (oral fluid or blood), performs the test, and interprets the result, often in a private setting, either alone or with someone they trust. 11. HIV-inconclusive status occurs when the testing strategy cannot definitively determine whether an individual is HIV-positive or HIV-negative. This is distinct from discrepant test results. 12. HIV testing services (HTS) encompass not only the testing itself but also related services such as pre-test information, post-test counseling, linkage to HIV prevention, care, and treatment services, and coordination with laboratory services to ensure quality assurance. 13. HIV status is the final interpretation of a patient’s disease state based on a collection of test results from one or more assays. It may be reported as HIV-positive, HIV-negative, or HIV-inconclusive. 14. A hotspot is a small area within a larger geographic region where HIV prevalence or incidence is particularly high. 15. An immunoassay is a method for detecting a substance (antigen) using an antibody that reacts specifically to it. 16. Index testing is a focused HIV testing approach where the household, family members (including children), and partners of individuals diagnosed with HIV are offered HTS. 17. Indicator condition-guided HIV testing targets individuals more likely to be infected with HIV based on specific conditions, such as lymphoma, cervical or anal neoplasia, or herpes zoster, which are more common in HIV-infected individuals. 18. Integration refers to the co-location and sharing of services and resources across different health service areas. For HIV, this may include testing, prevention, treatment, and care services alongside services for tuberculosis, sexually transmitted infections, hepatitis B/C, antenatal care, contraception, and other conditions. 19. An in vitro diagnostic medical device (IVD) is a medical device used to examine human specimens to provide information for diagnosis, monitoring, or determining compatibility. Examples include reagents, calibrators, control materials, specimen receptacles, and related instruments. 20. Intimate partner violence involves behaviors by one person in an intimate relationship that cause physical, psychological, or sexual harm to the other person, including physical violence, sexual violence, emotional abuse, and controlling behaviors. 21. Key populations are groups at increased risk of HIV due to specific high-risk behaviors, regardless of the epidemic type or local context. These include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, people in prisons, sex workers, and transgender individuals. 22. A lay provider is someone trained to deliver health-care services but lacks formal professional or para-professional certification or tertiary education. 23. Multi-analyte testing uses the same platform to test for different analytes with different sets of reagents, often requiring more than one specimen. 24. Multiplex testing involves testing a single specimen for multiple analytes using one test device, such as detecting HIV-1/2 antibodies and syphilis antibodies simultaneously. 25. Negative predictive value is the probability that a person with a negative test result is truly HIV-negative. 26. A non-reactive test result indicates no reaction suggesting the presence of an analyte, such as HIV-1 p24 antigen or HIV-1/2 antibodies. 27. Nucleic acid testing detects very small quantities of viral nucleic acids (RNA, DNA, or TNA) qualitatively and quantitatively, using molecular technologies like PCR or NASBA. 28. Partner services involve a voluntary process where a trained provider asks HIV-positive individuals about their sexual or drug-injecting partners and, with consent, offers HTS to those partners. 29. Patient referral is a partner services approach where HIV-positive clients are encouraged to disclose their status to their partners and suggest HTS to them. 30. A policy is an institutional statement guiding actions within a specific domain. 31. Positive predictive value is the probability that a person with a positive test result is truly HIV-positive. 32. Pre-test information is a concise dialogue providing accurate information to a client before an HIV test is performed. 33. Provider-assisted delayed referral involves an agreement between an HIV-positive client and a trained provider to disclose the client’s status to their partners and suggest HTS within a set time frame. If the partners do not access testing within this period, the provider contacts them directly to offer voluntary HTS. 34. Provider-assisted referral is when a trained provider helps HIV-positive clients share their status or anonymously inform their partners of potential HIV exposure and offers voluntary HTS to those partners. 35. Provider–patient referral involves a trained provider accompanying and supporting HIV-positive clients as they disclose their status and potential HIV exposure to their partners, followed by offering voluntary HTS. 36. Quality assurance ensures stakeholders that quality requirements will be met. 37. Quality control (QC) verifies that a product meets quality requirements and identifies defects to formally reject defective products. 38. Quality improvement (QI) involves proposing solutions to enhance quality and reliability, often using the plan/do/check/act cycle. 39. A quality management system directs and controls an organization’s efforts to meet quality objectives through systematic and process-oriented approaches. 40. A rapid diagnostic test (RDT) is an in vitro diagnostic device that detects HIV-1/2 antibodies and/or HIV p24 antigen using immunochromatographic or immunofiltration formats. 41. A reactive test result indicates a reaction suggesting the presence of an analyte, such as HIV-1 p24 antigen or HIV-1/2 antibodies. 42. Repeat testing involves additional testing during the same visit due to inconclusive or discrepant results, using the same assay and specimen where possible. 43. Retesting is the testing of a second specimen from the same individual using the same algorithm as a quality assurance step, performed at a later time. 44. Sensitivity is the probability that an HIV assay or algorithm correctly identifies all specimens containing HIV-1/2 antibodies and/or HIV-1 p24 antigen. 45. Analytical sensitivity refers to the smallest amount of analyte (antibodies or antigen) that an assay can accurately detect, including different subtypes like HIV-1 group O. 46. Diagnostic sensitivity is the percentage of HIV-infected individuals identified as HIV-positive by the assay or testing algorithm. 47. Seroconversion sensitivity is the ability of an assay to detect HIV infection as an individual undergoes seroconversion, with antibodies evolving from IgM to IgG. 48. Sentinel surveillance is conducted at selected sites among specific populations to approximate prevalence for a larger population, such as in antenatal clinics. 49. Seroconversion occurs when an individual’s immune system produces enough HIV-1/2 antibodies to be detectable by an HIV serology assay. 50. A serodiscordant couple is one in which one partner is HIV-positive and the other is HIV-negative. 51. A serology assay detects antibodies in human specimens, typically using serum or plasma but also capillary/venous whole blood or oral fluid. 52. Social network-based HIV testing extends partner services by encouraging individuals with HIV or at ongoing risk to invite members of their sexual, drug-injecting, or social networks to participate in voluntary HTS. 53. Specificity is the probability that an assay or algorithm correctly identifies specimens that do not contain HIV-1/2 antibodies and/or HIV-1 p24 antigen. 54. Analytical specificity is the ability of an assay to distinguish the relevant analyte from others, minimizing false reactivity. 55. Diagnostic specificity is the percentage of HIV-uninfected individuals identified as HIV-negative by the assay or testing algorithm. 56. A strategic plan translates policy into planned activities with strategic objectives, typically valid for one year in relation to a budget cycle. 57. Supplemental testing involves additional assays to obtain more information and ascertain HIV status. 58. Task sharing redistributes tasks between health-care providers with varying levels of training, such as trained lay providers. 59. Test for triage involves a single HIV RDT conducted by a trained provider, with reactive results referred to a health facility for confirmatory testing. 60. A testing algorithm specifies the products used in a testing strategy, including product names, codes, manufacturing sites, and regulatory versions. 61. A testing strategy is a sequence of tests conducted on assays to achieve specific objectives, such as screening or diagnosing infection. 62. Throughput refers to the number of tests performed within a given time frame.
